property_summary: For any caller and any timestamp/block, the reference contract accepts a fallback call only when msg.value == 10 ether (so calls with 10 ether succeed and update pastBlockTime), whereas the mutant requiring 9 ether will reject some calls that the reference accepts (calls with 10 ether) — the test fuzzes the sent value and caller to show a difference.

Invariant: each successful call to fallback with msg.value == 10 ether in the correct contract always increases pastBlockTime to the current block.timestamp only if block.timestamp is strictly greater than the previous pastBlockTime (so repeated calls in same block do not update pastBlockTime); the mutant that removed the time check can update pastBlockTime even when block.timestamp has not advanced, breaking that rule for some inputs (multiple calls within same block).

For any caller and any block timestamp, calling fallback with exactly 10 ether on the reference C never updates pastBlockTime if the call occurs in the same block time as the previous update (i.e., pastBlockTime only increases when block.timestamp > previous pastBlockTime); the mutant removed that time check and therefore can update pastBlockTime even when timestamp did not advance, so repeated calls within the same timestamp can make pastBlockTime change in the mutant but not in the reference.

For any caller and any block number/timestamp, if two calls to fallback with msg.value == 10 ether occur in the same block timestamp, the reference C will NOT transfer funds on the second call unless block.number % 15 == 0 and block.timestamp advanced (i.e. pastBlockTime is updated only when timestamp increases), whereas the mutant may update pastBlockTime on the second call in the same timestamp and thus may trigger a transfer that empties the contract balance; the test detects this by making two calls in the same timestamp and asserting that address(c).balance is unchanged (non-zero) after the second call in the reference but can become zero in the mutant.

Whenever fallback is called twice with exactly 10 ether from the same caller within the same block timestamp, the reference contract updates pastBlockTime only on the first call (so the second call cannot change pastBlockTime or cause the conditional transfer), while the mutant (which removed the timestamp check) can update pastBlockTime on the second call and thereby may trigger the transfer and change address(c).balance.

For any caller and any block timestamp, calling fallback with exactly 10 ether never makes pastBlockTime decrease and never changes when called with the same block.timestamp if it was already equal to that timestamp (i.e., pastBlockTime only updates when block.timestamp strictly increases); the mutant (which removed the require) can update pastBlockTime even when block.timestamp did not increase, so for some inputs a second call in the same block timestamp will change pastBlockTime in the mutant but not in the reference.

After any successful fallback call that sends exactly 10 ether and has block.timestamp > pastBlockTime, the contract's public pastBlockTime is updated to the final block.timestamp; the mutant that delays the store until after a conditional transfer can leave pastBlockTime unchanged when the transfer drains the contract (via a reentrancy/transfer behaviour), violating this invariant for some inputs.

For any caller sending exactly 10 ether when block.timestamp > pastBlockTime, C always updates its public pastBlockTime to the current block.timestamp after fallback returns; the mutant that defers the update until after a conditional transfer can allow a reentrant draining transfer to execute and leave pastBlockTime unchanged, breaking this property for some inputs.

For any caller that sends exactly 10 ether when block.timestamp > pastBlockTime and when the block number is a multiple of 15, the reference contract always updates its public pastBlockTime to block.timestamp after the fallback call returns; the mutant that defers the update until after a conditional transfer can be exploited by a reentrant attacker to drain the balance before the store, leaving pastBlockTime unchanged and thus violating the property for some inputs.

For any caller that sends exactly 10 ether when block.timestamp > pastBlockTime, after fallback returns the contract's public pastBlockTime equals the call's block.timestamp; the mutant that defers the store until after a conditional transfer can be exploited by a reentrant attacker (which drains the balance during the conditional transfer) to leave pastBlockTime unchanged, violating this invariant for some inputs.

For any caller sending exactly 10 ether when block.timestamp > pastBlockTime, after a successful fallback call the contract's public pastBlockTime is strictly updated to the current block.timestamp; the mutant that defers the store until after a conditional transfer can be reentrancy-exploited during the transfer to leave pastBlockTime unchanged, violating this rule for some inputs.

For any caller sending exactly 10 ether to fallback at a strictly later timestamp, the reference contract only transfers its balance to the caller when block.number % 15 == 0 (so address(c).balance == 0 after the call iff block.number % 15 == 0); the mutant flips the condition and thus will make address(c).balance == 0 for block.number % 15 != 0, so there exist block numbers (fuzzed) where the observed post-call balance differs.

For any call to fallback that sends exactly 10 ether and occurs at a strictly later timestamp than the previous call, whenever block.number % 15 == 0 the reference contract forwards the entire contract balance to msg.sender (leaving c.balance == 0) while the mutant may leave a non-zero balance (breaking the rule).
